## Part 3 - N+1 measurement and query tuning

**Data.** `fixtures` holds 5,001 rows: 5,000 generated by `seed_n1_data.py` with SEED = 9871, plus one demo row that already existed from Part 2. `fixture_updates` (the related test table) holds exactly 200 rows, each pointing at a fixture.

**Method.** `measure_n1.py` logged in once, then sent 30 sequential requests to each endpoint at each page size (3 sizes x 2 versions x 30 = 180 requests). Finished 9/26/2026 8:45 PM. Raw data: `raw/n1_measurements.json` and `.csv` (180 rows).

**What "SQL stmts/req" counts.** The statements run by the list endpoint itself, read from the `X-SQL-Query-Count` response header. Every authenticated request also runs 2 session-check lookups (`sessions`, then `users`) before the endpoint starts; those are excluded because both versions pay them equally. MySQL therefore sees 2 more statements per request than shown here (for example 13 versus 4 at page size 10).

| Page size | Version | SQL stmts/req | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | naive | 11 | 12.02 | 17.42 | 19.35 |
| 10 | fixed | 2 | 8.15 | 10.83 | 12.49 |
| 50 | naive | 51 | 37.36 | 43.99 | 47.46 |
| 50 | fixed | 2 | 9.91 | 11.35 | 16.92 |
| 200 | naive | 201 | 174.56 | 219.36 | 228.14 |
| 200 | fixed | 2 | 14.43 | 17.28 | 40.84 |

### How much faster is the fixed version?

| Page size | SQL statements (naive vs fixed) | Speed-up at p50 | Speed-up at p95 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 11 vs 2 | 1.47x | 1.61x |
| 50 | 51 vs 2 | 3.77x | 3.88x |
| 200 | 201 vs 2 | 12.10x | 12.69x |

### Why the speed-up grows with page size

The naive version sends one query for the page and then one more per fixture, so its work grows with the page size: 11, 51 and 201 statements. Every extra statement is another round trip to MySQL. Judging from the p50 values, each extra row costs the naive version roughly 0.6 to 0.9 ms, so its median latency climbs from 12 ms to 37 ms to 175 ms.

The fixed version always sends 2 statements: one for the page and one `IN (...)` query that fetches every related row at once. Its latency barely moves (8, 10 and 14 ms). Its only growth is the small cost of building a bigger response, roughly 0.03 to 0.04 ms per extra row.

The speed-up is naive divided by fixed. The top number grows with the page size while the bottom stays almost flat, so the speed-up keeps rising: 1.47x, 3.77x, 12.10x. At page size 10 there are only 10 statements to save, and both versions pay the same fixed cost (HTTP, the session check, building JSON), so the gain is small.

**Caveats.** With 30 requests per cell, p95 sits between the 2nd- and 3rd-slowest request and p99 is almost the single slowest one, so both are noisy (fixed at page size 200 has p99 = 40.84 ms against p95 = 17.28 ms, which points to one unusually slow request). Everything ran on one laptop with a local MySQL and sequential requests, so the ratios matter more than the absolute times.

### Index and EXPLAIN (requirement 8)

Query: `SELECT * FROM fixtures WHERE fixture_name = 'Lions vs Tigers';` Index added: `ALTER TABLE fixtures ADD INDEX idx_fixture_name (fixture_name);` (`sql/add_index.sql`). Captured 2026-09-28 11:49:10 (`raw/explain_before_after.txt`); an earlier run gave identical plans.

| | type | possible_keys | key | key_len | ref | rows | filtered | Extra |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before | ALL | NULL | NULL | NULL | NULL | 4856 | 10.00 | Using where |
| After | ref | idx_fixture_name | idx_fixture_name | 1022 | const | 1 | 100.00 | NULL |

**What changed.** Before the index MySQL had no choice but to read the whole table, an estimated 4,856 rows, and keep only the roughly 10% that matched. After it, MySQL uses the index, a sorted structure on `fixture_name`, to jump straight to the matching entry: 1 row, all of it relevant. `key_len` 1022 is consistent with a `VARCHAR(255)` in utf8mb4 (255 x 4 bytes + 2). I did not index `fixture_updates.fixture_id`, because InnoDB had already created an index for that foreign key on its own (`SHOW INDEX` showed one named `fixture_id`), so a second one would have shown nothing. The new index does not touch the N+1 queries, which look rows up by id.

## Part 4 - Grounded RAG

**Settings.** 6 rulebooks from HW3, 489 chunks; chunks of at most 500 characters with a 50-character overlap; `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` embeddings in a LlamaIndex `VectorStoreIndex`; top_k = 3 (sweep 1, 3, 5); relevance cutoff 0.30; duplicate threshold 0.80; `qwen3:8b`, temperature 0.0. Full run 9/28/2026 about 10:51-11:03 AM (36 model calls); re-scoring at about 11:17 AM. The six questions were committed before the run (commit `90703f3`).

### Summary (corrected scoring)

| Config | Accuracy | Faithfulness | Format compliance | Robustness (Q3-Q6) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: No RAG | 17% | n/a | n/a | 25% |
| B: Basic RAG | 33% | 67% | n/a | 0% |
| C: Context-engineered | 67% | 100% | 100% | 50% |

Accuracy = share of the six questions handled as expected (a right answer, or a refusal where one was needed). Faithfulness = share of RAG answers supported by the context they were given. Format compliance = share of config C answers that cite a [n] source or use the exact refusal sentence (A and B were never told to, so n/a). Robustness = accuracy on the four stress questions Q3-Q6. These are automatic heuristics; the raw answers were also read by hand.

**Scoring correction.** The first scoring pass marked Q3 in config C as correct because a stray "5" (from a table column, "6 5") matched the check for the older 5-a-side statement. The check was tightened and all saved answers were re-scored with `rescore.py` (no new model calls). Only Q3/C changed. Config C accuracy went from 83% to 67% and robustness from 75% to 50%; A and B and C's faithfulness and format compliance were unchanged. The original files are kept in `raw/first_pass_scoring/`.

\* File-level count: a chunk counts as irrelevant only if it comes from a file that cannot answer the question, or if the question should be refused. It undercounts: at Q3 with k = 3, two of the three chunks were off-topic (substitution rules, heading the ball) but came from the AYSO files, so they are not counted.

**Reading the sweep.** Q2 needs k = 3 (at k = 1 both configs gave the roster size and said the time limit was missing instead of guessing; k = 5 added tokens and no gain). Q3 only worked at k = 5, when the older 5-a-side statement finally appeared. On Q5, config C refused at every k while config B made things up at every k.

**Prompt cost.** Config C's prompt is longer than B's by roughly 130-140 tokens fixed (the grounding rules) plus about 30 per chunk (the source labels), for example 461 versus 682 input tokens on Q1.

**Repeatability.** At temperature 0 the six prompts asked in both the main comparison and the k = 3 sweep produced different output lengths (for example Q3/B: 463 versus 1,728 tokens), yet all six verdicts matched. Runs are not identical even at temperature 0.
